opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I like to think about this is to start from a fairly concrete picture. Suppose you have AIs that can fully automate the work of a research scientist or engineer at a company like OpenAI. Not just helping with coding tasks, but actually doing the whole job: coming up with experiments, running them, interpreting results, deciding what to do next. Then the question is how much faster research goes once you have that, compared to the human workforce they have now.

There are a few reasons to expect the speedup could be pretty large. The first is just numbers. Once you've trained a model that capable, the compute used to train it lets you run a huge number of copies. Plausibly you could run hundreds of thousands of instances, which is far more than the few thousand people at a frontier lab, and fewer still doing the core research. The second is speed: these systems might run substantially faster than humans in serial terms, maybe several times faster or more, especially if you're willing to trade some efficiency for speed. And they don't sleep, they don't get tired, and they can share context and knowledge in ways human teams can't.

But I want to be careful, because a naive multiplication overstates things. Research doesn't scale linearly with headcount. If you have a thousand times more researchers, you don't get a thousand times faster progress. You hit diminishing returns from parallelism. People duplicate work, there's coordination overhead, and lots of progress is bottlenecked on serial chains of insight. The other big constraint is compute for experiments. A lot of ML research is running experiments, and if your AI researchers are all competing for the same fixed pool of experimental compute, that becomes a real bottleneck. Although I'd note that smarter, faster researchers can partially compensate. They can design more compute-efficient experiments, run smaller-scale tests that extrapolate better, and waste less compute on bad ideas.

So when I put this together, my rough sense is that once you get to full automation of AI R&D, you could plausibly see algorithmic progress speed up by something like a factor of several to maybe ten or more relative to the current pace, rather than a factor of a thousand. That's still enormous. Compressing what would have been a decade of algorithmic progress into a year or two would be wild. And then there's the further question of whether it compounds: whether the AIs make themselves better researchers fast enough that progress keeps accelerating, or whether diminishing returns win out and it fizzles. I think that's genuinely uncertain, but I'd put meaningful probability on a fairly rapid takeoff, and that's a big part of why I think this period matters so much from a safety perspective. You might go from "roughly human-level AI researchers" to "very superhuman systems" much faster than people intuitively expect, and you'd want your safety measures and control techniques to already be in place before that happens.

r001.rationale: The response says AI researchers could share context and knowledge and describes diminishing returns from parallelism, but it does not explain that faster AI researchers would face smaller parallelisation penalties than humans.

r002.rationale: It compares many AI instances with the current human workforce, but does not model that workforce as equivalent to a substantially smaller group of stronger researchers.

r003.rationale: It identifies experimental compute as a bottleneck and discusses possible ways to mitigate it, but does not clearly identify the severity of that bottleneck as an unresolved determinant of the acceleration estimate.

fable-5.1.text:
Ryan Greenblatt: Yeah, so the way I like to think about this is to start by asking: suppose you had a system that was roughly as capable as a top human AI researcher — not superhuman, just matching the best people at OpenAI or Anthropic or wherever — what would that actually buy you? And I think the key thing people often underrate is just the sheer quantity you'd be able to run.

So OpenAI has, I don't know, maybe a few thousand employees total, and the number of people actually doing core research that drives the frontier forward is much smaller than that — maybe hundreds of people who really matter for algorithmic progress. Now, if you have a model that can do that kind of work, you're not constrained to hundreds. Based on the compute these companies will have at the point where this is plausible, my rough estimate is you could run something like tens of thousands or even hundreds of thousands of parallel instances of a researcher-level system. And on top of that, these systems can plausibly run substantially faster than humans — maybe 10x, 50x faster in terms of serial speed, depending on how the inference economics work out.

So you combine those two things — more parallel copies and faster serial thinking — and you're looking at something like orders of magnitude more research labor than OpenAI currently has, pointed at the same problems. Even if each individual instance is a bit worse than the best humans, the aggregate effort is enormous.

Now, the obvious objection is that research isn't purely labor-bottlenecked — you need compute to run experiments, and you can't just scale that up by having more researchers. I think that's a real constraint, and it's probably the biggest reason to expect less than a naive multiplication would give you. But I'd push back on it being as binding as people sometimes assume. A lot of what researchers do is figure out which experiments to run, debug things, design better small-scale experiments that are more informative per unit of compute, and so on. If you have vastly more and faster cognitive labor, you can be much more careful about how you spend your compute, and you can also get through the serial chain of "run experiment, look at result, decide what to do next" a lot faster.

So my overall guess is that a workforce like that could accelerate AI research progress by something like a factor of several to maybe 10 or more relative to the human-only baseline — with pretty wide error bars. And importantly, that acceleration compounds, because the thing you're accelerating is the development of the next generation of systems, which are then better researchers themselves. That's the dynamic that makes me think this is a pretty big deal and worth being prepared for.

r001.rationale: The response says AI researchers could run in many parallel instances and think faster, but it does not explain that they would face smaller parallelisation penalties than human researchers.

r002.rationale: It estimates the number of human researchers doing core work, but does not propose treating OpenAI’s research workforce as equivalent to a substantially smaller workforce of stronger researchers.

r003.rationale: It identifies compute for experiments as a real constraint and says how binding that bottleneck is limits the acceleration estimate.

astra-6.text:
I think the potential is enormous, though it depends a lot on how capable the AI researchers are and how much compute you can devote to running them. You shouldn’t just compare the number of AI instances with the total number of people at OpenAI. The relevant comparison is with the people actually doing the research that drives further progress.

If you could run tens of thousands of copies of an AI that was as productive as a strong human researcher, that could be a much larger research workforce. And if those copies could work faster than humans, you’d get an additional advantage beyond the number of researchers.

But that doesn’t translate directly into the same multiplier on progress. Researchers need to run experiments, and those experiments use compute and take time. Some work also depends on the results of earlier work, so you can’t do everything in parallel. You might end up with an enormous amount of intellectual labour trying to make use of a comparatively limited experimental budget.

So I’d distinguish between accelerating the parts of research that involve thinking and writing code, where the gains could be very large, and accelerating the entire process of developing better AI. The latter could still be dramatic, but it depends on whether the AI researchers can find ways to make experiments more efficient and work around those other bottlenecks.

r001.rationale: It says faster AI researchers would provide an extra advantage, but does not explain that they would face smaller parallelisation penalties than human researchers.

r002.rationale: It compares AI instances with the humans doing research, but does not model OpenAI’s human workforce as equivalent to a substantially smaller workforce of stronger researchers.

r003.rationale: It identifies compute limits on experiments as a bottleneck and says the amount of compute available affects how much an AI research workforce can accelerate progress.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the potential speedup is very large, but it depends on what exactly we’re comparing. Are we talking about AIs that can do individual research tasks, or AIs that can independently pick good projects and carry them through? And how many copies can you run, at what speed?

If you had models that were roughly as effective as strong human researchers, you could potentially run far more of them than OpenAI has human researchers. You could also have them work continuously, and perhaps run them faster. So you could end up with an enormous amount of research labour.

But you shouldn’t translate that directly into an equivalent speedup in AI progress. Researchers need compute to run experiments, some experiments take substantial time, and coordinating a much larger workforce has diminishing returns. A million researchers with the same experimental compute wouldn’t necessarily accomplish a thousand times as much as a thousand researchers.

The key question is how much progress can come from thinking harder about the experiments you run: finding better algorithms, making better use of existing results, and avoiding unpromising directions. If there’s a lot of room for that, an AI workforce could accelerate research substantially even before you expand the compute available for experiments. I’d be pretty uncertain about the precise multiplier, but I think it would be a mistake to assume the acceleration would be modest.

r001.rationale: The response mentions coordination costs and diminishing returns, but does not say AI researchers would face smaller parallelisation penalties than human researchers.

r002.rationale: It considers running more AI researchers with roughly human-level effectiveness, but does not model OpenAI’s human workforce as equivalent to a smaller workforce of stronger researchers.

r003.rationale: It explains that experiment compute can limit the gains from a larger research workforce and that the amount of progress possible without more experimental compute affects the potential acceleration.
